name: Brabo Choke
description: Master the Brabo Choke in BJJ. Complete guide with safety protocols, setup from front headlock, execution steps. Success rates: Beginner 35%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
variant_uniqueness: Arm-in choke using opponent's shoulder as compression point
summary: The Brabo Choke is an arm-in blood choke from the front headlock and top pins where you thread an arm across the opponent's neck and trap their own near-side shoulder against it, compressing the carotid arteries until they tap.
overview: The Brabo Choke is a powerful blood choke from the front headlock position, closely related to the Darce and Anaconda chokes. The technique involves threading your arm under the opponent's near arm and across their neck, securing a grip on your own bicep to create a vice-like constriction of the carotid arteries. The name 'Brabo' is a Portuguese pronunciation variation of 'Darce,' though some practitioners distinguish between the two based on subtle grip and angle differences. This submission is particularly effective when the opponent is defending a front headlock by keeping their elbows tight, creating the necessary space for arm insertion. The Brabo Choke excels in scramble situations, turtle attacks, and failed takedown defense scenarios. Its effectiveness comes from the mechanical advantage created by using your entire body weight to compress the opponent's neck against their own shoulder, making it extremely difficult to defend once properly locked. The choke works in both gi and no-gi contexts, though grip variations differ slightly between formats. Modern competitors favor this submission for its high finishing rate and the control it provides throughout the execution process.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression causing loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for serious injury if held after unconsciousness

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain or cervical spine stress from improper angle
Shoulder impingement from trapped arm position
Trachea damage from improper forearm placement
injury_risks.recovery_time: 2-6 weeks or longer; potential permanent damage

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum pressure buildup in training
tap_signals: Verbal tap or any vocal distress signal
Multiple taps with free hand on opponent's body
Multiple taps with feet on the mat
Any unusual sound or movement indicating distress
Loss of resistance or body going limp (IMMEDIATE RELEASE)
release_protocol: Immediately release the choking arm grip upon tap signal
Remove arm from under opponent's neck smoothly (do not jerk)
Allow opponent to expand neck and breathe freely
Check partner's condition and allow recovery time before continuing
If partner was close to unconsciousness, extend rest period to 2-3 minutes minimum
training_restrictions: Never apply sudden or jerking pressure to the neck
Never use competition finishing speed during training rolls
Never continue pressure after tap signal for any reason
Never practice on opponents with known neck or spinal injuries without explicit medical clearance
Never hold the choke 'just to see' if partner will tap - always release at first signal
Avoid practicing at full intensity until proper technique is established (minimum 20+ controlled repetitions)

variations_and_setups.description: When opponent turtles, establish front headlock control and thread arm under their near arm before they can strengthen defensive posture. The turtle position provides excellent setup opportunity.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Opponent turtles to defend guard pass or takedown; very common in competition

variations_and_setups.description: After failed takedown attempt when you're stuck in front headlock, thread the Brabo and use opponent's forward pressure to roll them over you, landing in top position with choke locked.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Your takedown is defended and opponent has strong sprawl pressure

variations_and_setups.description: From side control, if opponent turns into you to escape, capture front headlock and immediately thread Brabo before they complete the turn.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Opponent attempts to turn toward you during side control escape

variations_and_setups.description: From standing clinch, fake guillotine entry to get opponent to defend, then switch to Brabo arm thread when they hand fight the guillotine.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Standing grappling exchanges when opponent is guillotine-aware

variations_and_setups.description: Instead of standard bicep grip, bring your elbow high above opponent's back and grip your own wrist, creating different angle of pressure. More common in no-gi.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Standard grip is difficult to secure or opponent is defending traditional angle
